subtopic_detail: Choosing a scabicide that is age appropriate for a young infant while treating the household
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6 week old boy whose parents say he has been squirming and crying for the past fortnight and has a rash that is spreading.

He has small red bumps and some blistery spots across his trunk, and his mother shows you the same spots on the soles of both feet, the palms of both hands and across his scalp. Both parents describe intense itching at night that keeps them awake, and you can see thin wavy lines between the fingers of the mother's right hand. The baby is feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile and has no fever. There is no honey coloured crusting and no surrounding spreading redness.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous papules and vesicopustules over trunk, palms, soles and scalp, burrows visible in the mother's finger web spaces, no impetiginised crusting, no cellulitis, weight tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Oral ivermectin for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
options.rationale: Ivermectin is not used in children under 15 kg or under five years because safety data are lacking, and it is a second line agent even in adults with ordinary scabies (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Topical corticosteroid for the baby and permethrin for the parents
options.rationale: A corticosteroid settles the itch but leaves the mite in place and allows continued transmission, and unopposed steroid can convert ordinary scabies to the crusted form (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Oral cefalexin for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment is added when there is secondary bacterial infection with honey coloured crusting or surrounding cellulitis, and neither is present on this examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Sulfur ointment for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
options.rationale: Permethrin is not recommended below two months of age in Australia, so sulfur in a soft paraffin base applied for three consecutive nights is the preferred scabicide for this infant, while all household members are treated simultaneously whether or not they are itching (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Permethrin 5 per cent cream for the baby and all household contacts
options.rationale: Permethrin is the correct agent for everyone else in this household but is outside its approved age range for a 6 week old, which is the specific reason the infant needs a different preparation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult pattern in distribution: the scalp, face, palms and soles are involved in babies and spared in older children and adults, and vesicles and pustules are far more common. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by finding burrows in a household contact, and treatment failure is far more often due to untreated contacts or incorrect application than to genuine resistance. Every household member and every recent close physical contact is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms, because the incubation period before itching starts is up to six weeks in a first infestation. Itch persists for two to four weeks after successful treatment because it is a hypersensitivity response to mite antigen, and this is the commonest reason families believe treatment has failed and re treat unnecessarily.
key_points: Infants have scalp, face, palm and sole involvement that older children do not.
Permethrin is not recommended below two months of age in Australia.
All household and close contacts are treated on the same day regardless of symptoms.
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and does not indicate treatment failure.
Application must cover the entire body including under the nails, and be left on overnight.
explanation.pearls: Bedding, towels and clothing used in the previous two days need hot washing or sealing in a plastic bag for at least three days, because the mite survives away from skin for around 24 to 36 hours at room temperature.

subtopic_detail: Reading periorbital bruising with an abdominal mass as metastatic disease rather than injury
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3 year old girl whose mother felt a lump in her tummy while bathing her three days ago.

Over the past month she has been pale and grizzly, has stopped wanting to walk to the park and has been limping on and off without any fall the family can recall. She has purple discolouration around both eyes that her mother assumed came from tripping over a toy a fortnight ago. On examination there is a firm irregular mass in the left upper abdomen that extends across the midline and does not move with respiration. Her blood pressure is normal for age and there is no blood on urine dipstick.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular fixed abdominal mass extending across the midline, bilateral periorbital ecchymoses with no lid swelling or tenderness, pallor, no hepatomegaly, antalgic gait
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), urine dipstick negative for blood and protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a full blood count and arrange orthopaedic review of the limp
options.rationale: The blood count is already available and shows an anaemia that needs explaining, and treating the limp as an isolated orthopaedic problem ignores the abdominal mass that unifies the presentation (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Arrange coagulation studies and review the bruising in one week
options.rationale: A coagulopathy would produce bruising at varied sites rather than a symmetrical periocular distribution, and the platelet count is normal, so this pathway would waste a week (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Send urinary catecholamine metabolites and arrange abdominal imaging
options.rationale: A fixed irregular mass crossing the midline with bone pain, anaemia and bilateral periorbital bruising from orbital bone metastases indicates a catecholamine secreting tumour of neural crest origin, and urinary homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid with cross sectional imaging is the pathway (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Arrange abdominal ultrasound and send urine for microscopy only
options.rationale: The near pair is a renal embryonal tumour, which characteristically gives a smooth mass that does not cross the midline, with hypertension and haematuria, and neither the blood pressure nor the dipstick supports it here (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey for non accidental injury before imaging
options.rationale: Bilateral symmetrical periorbital bruising without lid swelling or tenderness is characteristic of orbital metastatic deposits rather than trauma, and attributing it to injury is the classic delay in this diagnosis (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood, with a median age at diagnosis of around 18 months, and more than half of children have metastatic disease when they present. It arises anywhere along the sympathetic chain, most often in the adrenal gland, and the abdominal mass characteristically crosses the midline because it originates retroperitoneally rather than within an organ. Bone and bone marrow are the commonest metastatic sites, producing pain, limp, pallor and the striking bilateral periorbital ecchymoses that come from orbital bone deposits. Around 90 per cent of tumours secrete catecholamines, so urinary metabolites provide a simple non invasive screening test, and staging uses meta iodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy alongside cross sectional imaging.
key_points: A mass crossing the midline and fixed to the retroperitoneum suggests neural crest rather than renal origin.
Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis without swelling reflects orbital bone metastases.
Around 90 per cent of tumours secrete catecholamines detectable in urine.
The renal embryonal tumour gives a smooth mass that respects the midline, with hypertension and haematuria.
Bone and marrow are the commonest metastatic sites, causing limp, pain and anaemia.
explanation.pearls: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome, with chaotic eye movements and jerky limb movements, is a paraneoplastic presentation that occurs in around two per cent of children and can appear before any mass is palpable, so it always prompts a search for an occult neuroblastoma.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Treating household threadworm when the index child is below the age threshold for anthelmintics
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 month old girl whose 4 year old brother was diagnosed with threadworm a week ago and treated at the pharmacy.

Her mother says the baby has been waking and squirming after midnight for the past four nights, and two nights ago she saw several fine white threads moving around the baby's bottom when she changed her. The baby is feeding well and has gained weight along her centile line. There is no diarrhoea, no blood in the nappy and no fever. The perianal skin is slightly red from scratching with no discharge, no ulceration and no crusting.

data_table.Examination: Mild perianal erythema, no excoriation breach, no discharge, no lymphadenopathy, weight tracking along the 40th centile
data_table.Investigations: Household of five including two adults and three children aged 5 months, 4 years and 7 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Permethrin cream for the baby and mebendazole for the household
options.rationale: Permethrin is a topical scabicide with no activity against intestinal helminths, so it targets the wrong organism entirely despite also being a nocturnal itch treatment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Faecal microscopy for the baby before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Eggs are deposited on perianal skin rather than passed in faeces, so stool microscopy is insensitive and unnecessary when adult worms have already been seen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Hygiene measures for the baby and mebendazole for the household
options.rationale: Anthelmintic treatment is not recommended below six months of age, so this infant is managed with hygiene measures alone while every other household member is treated simultaneously to remove the reservoir that keeps reinfecting her (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Mebendazole for the baby and for all household members now
options.rationale: Treating the whole household simultaneously is correct, but mebendazole is outside its recommended age range at five months and safety data below six months are inadequate (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Mebendazole for the baby now and a repeat dose in two weeks
options.rationale: The two week repeat dose is the correct schedule because the drug does not kill eggs, but it compounds rather than corrects the age problem and leaves the rest of the household untreated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Threadworm is extremely common in Australian households with young children and spreads by the faecal to oral route when eggs deposited on perianal skin at night are transferred to hands, bedding and surfaces. Eggs remain viable in the environment for two to three weeks, which is why a single dose fails and why the whole household is treated together with a repeat dose two weeks later. Diagnosis is made by seeing the worms, usually two to three hours after the child falls asleep, or by an adhesive tape preparation applied to the perianal skin in the morning; stool examination is unhelpful. In infants below the treatment age threshold, the practical approach is to eliminate the reservoir in the rest of the household and rely on hygiene measures until the child is old enough.
key_points: Anthelmintic treatment is not recommended below six months of age.
All household members are treated at the same time, with a repeat dose after two weeks.
The drug kills adult worms but not eggs, which is why the repeat dose is needed.
Eggs are laid on perianal skin, so stool microscopy is insensitive.
Hygiene measures cover morning bathing, nail trimming, handwashing and hot washing of bedding.
explanation.pearls: In girls, migrating worms can reach the vulva and cause vulvovaginitis or recurrent urinary symptoms, so nocturnal perianal itch in a girl presenting with unexplained vulval irritation is worth asking about before urine is sent.

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dose and quantification after a mid pregnancy sensitising event
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 28 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 20 weeks and 3 days who slipped on wet steps yesterday evening and struck her abdomen against the handrail.

She presents 18 hours later because a friend told her she should be checked. She has had no vaginal bleeding, no leaking and no abdominal pain since the fall, and she reports normal foetal movements. Her booking bloods recorded blood group O with a negative red cell antibody screen, and she has not yet had any anti-D this pregnancy. Her uterus is soft and non tender, and the foetal heart rate is 148 beats per minute on hand held Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, red cell antibody screen negative at booking, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165)
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender uterus, fundal height consistent with dates, no bruising over the abdominal wall, no vaginal bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give 625 IU anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer test
options.rationale: Abdominal trauma after 12 weeks is a sensitising event requiring 625 IU of anti-D as soon as possible and within 72 hours, with a quantification test sent at the same time to determine whether the bleed was large enough to need additional doses (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Give 250 IU anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer test
options.rationale: The 250 IU dose is the correct one for sensitising events in the first trimester, and using it after 12 weeks under doses a pregnancy in which the foetal red cell volume is considerably larger (Source: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give anti-D only if the result is raised
options.rationale: The quantification test determines whether extra doses are needed, not whether the standard dose is given, and waiting for the result erodes the 72 hour window in which prophylaxis is effective (Source: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D because more than 12 hours have already elapsed
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is given up to 72 hours after the event and is still worth giving beyond that if it has been missed, so an 18 hour delay is well inside the effective window (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Repeat the antibody screen and give anti-D if it is still negative
options.rationale: A repeat screen cannot be interpreted usefully at this point because passively acquired anti-D from prophylaxis is indistinguishable from immune anti-D on the screen, and delaying for the result serves no purpose (Source: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D alloimmunisation is prevented by giving anti-D immunoglobulin both routinely in the third trimester and after any potentially sensitising event. Sensitising events include abdominal trauma, antepartum haemorrhage, external cephalic version, invasive prenatal procedures, miscarriage and termination, and the dose depends on gestation: 250 IU up to 12 weeks and 625 IU thereafter. Routine antenatal prophylaxis in Australia is given as 625 IU at 28 and again at 34 weeks, and this is additional to rather than instead of event based doses. Quantification of foeto maternal haemorrhage after events beyond 20 weeks determines whether the standard dose is adequate, since a large bleed requires further immunoglobulin calculated on the measured volume.
key_points: Anti-D is given within 72 hours of a sensitising event and remains worth giving if missed.
The dose is 250 IU up to 12 weeks and 625 IU after 12 weeks.
Quantification of foeto maternal haemorrhage decides whether extra doses are needed.
Routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is additional to event based doses.
Cord blood grouping after birth determines whether a postnatal dose is required.
explanation.pearls: Non invasive foetal RhD genotyping on maternal plasma is now available in Australia and can spare an RhD negative woman carrying an RhD negative foetus from prophylaxis altogether, but where it is unavailable prophylaxis proceeds on the assumption that the foetus is RhD positive.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Fertility sparing management of atypical endometrial hyperplasia with intensive surveillance
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman in clinic with the result of an endometrial pipelle biopsy taken three weeks ago for eight months of heavy irregular bleeding.

She has polycystic ovary syndrome with a lifelong pattern of four or five periods a year, a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 and no other medical history. She has one child, conceived after ovulation induction, and she and her partner have been trying for a second for the past two years. The histology reports endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis shows an endometrium of 16 mm with no myometrial invasion, no cervical involvement and normal adnexa, and there is no lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, bulky mobile uterus, no adnexal masses, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial biopsy showing hyperplasia with atypia, magnetic resonance imaging with endometrial thickness 16 mm and no myometrial invasion, haemoglobin 106 g/L (115-165), ferritin 12 mcg/L (20-200)

options.text: Observation with repeat endometrial sampling again in 12 months
options.rationale: Atypical hyperplasia progresses to carcinoma in a substantial proportion within a few years, so observation without treatment is not an option even when fertility is being preserved (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: A levonorgestrel intrauterine system with three monthly sampling
options.rationale: For a woman who has not completed her family, high dose local progestogen delivered by intrauterine system achieves higher regression rates than oral progestogen and is combined with endometrial sampling every three months until two consecutive negative biopsies are obtained (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo oophorectomy as planned
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the standard treatment for atypical hyperplasia in a woman who has completed her family, but oophorectomy in a 42 year old is not routine, and proceeding to surgery forecloses the pregnancy she is actively seeking (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone with sampling again in one year
options.rationale: Cyclical rather than continuous dosing is inadequate for atypical disease, and a twelve month surveillance interval is far too long when up to 40 per cent harbour a concurrent carcinoma (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive with sampling again in six months
options.rationale: Combined contraception provides insufficient progestogenic opposition for established atypia and carries additional risk at a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia is classified as with or without atypia, and that single distinction drives everything: hyperplasia without atypia has a progression risk under five per cent over 20 years and is treated with progestogen, while atypical hyperplasia carries a concurrent carcinoma rate of up to 40 per cent at hysterectomy and a high progression risk. Standard management of atypia is total hysterectomy, with the ovaries usually conserved in premenopausal women. Fertility sparing treatment is legitimate but is a specialist decision requiring imaging to exclude invasive disease, high dose progestogen and intensive sampling every three months until regression is confirmed twice, followed by prompt referral for assisted conception because relapse rates after treatment are high. Weight loss and treatment of insulin resistance are part of the plan, since unopposed oestrogen from peripheral aromatisation and anovulation is what generated the lesion.
key_points: Atypia carries up to a 40 per cent rate of concurrent carcinoma at hysterectomy.
Hysterectomy is standard once the family is complete; ovaries are usually conserved before menopause.
Fertility sparing treatment uses the intrauterine progestogen system with three monthly sampling.
Two consecutive negative biopsies are required before conception is attempted.
Weight loss and management of anovulation address the underlying oestrogen excess.
explanation.pearls: After successful regression on fertility sparing treatment, referral for assisted conception is made without delay because relapse occurs in around a quarter within two years, and hysterectomy is recommended once childbearing is complete.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
